title: Students Need Struggle
author: Rebecca Hopersberger
summary: Rebecca Hopersberger, a former public school teacher now working in Catholic classical education, argues that struggle is a natural and necessary part of growth and that schools and parents too often shield children from it. She opens with Jacob wrestling in Scripture and notes that we cheer a toddler's shaky steps yet treat school difficulty as something to be removed or propped up with supports. Her diagnosis is that consumerism, the accreditation grift and social media vanity have corrupted what schooling is for, leaving parents anxious and eager to fix the system. She says anxious teenagers need low-stakes experiences of failure, and that a failing grade is a low-stakes event compared with salvation. Parents should model righteous struggle, pick their battles, and put children in the care of virtuous teachers with a sound curriculum.
points: Children build fortitude only when given agency to contend with hard material, so mediating every challenge produces a child who lacks confidence.
Consumerism, credential obsession and social media vanity have distorted education into something purchased and displayed rather than struggled for.
Part of the teenage anxiety crisis is an inability to handle failure, which parents worsen when they doom-spiral or mount a crusade over every setback.
Low-stakes failures such as a bad grade are the practice ground for the genuinely high-stakes matters of life, so they should be treated as such.
Adults model struggle by choosing battles well, and fighting over school board procedure is often the wrong fight compared with securing a good curriculum and virtuous teachers.
quotes: Children cannot grow in fortitude if they are not granted the agency to contend with challenging material and situations. The temptation to mediate each challenge your child faces will only lead to a child who lacks confidence.

It is a curious facet of our contemporary approach to education that when a student struggles in school, we find it necessary to either shield them from the difficulty, or provide them with “supports” that are the equivalent of brushing your ten-year-old’s teeth for them.

Consumerism has led to the idea that a good education can be bought irrespective of a student’s buy-in, and that the purchaser should get what they want. The accreditation grift has convinced the masses that a certificate is an accurate measure of a well-formed mind.
When young people are not lovingly supported through hard things, they become afraid of those hard things.

It is vital that children have enough experiences in low-stakes interactions to prepare them to function in the community at large. Contrary to popular sentiment, a failing grade is a low-stakes scenario, as is missing out on any number of secular rite-of-passage events.
Engaging in conflict for the sake of conflict, or on the wrong grounds, does not help our young people understand when and how to struggle.
Dale Ahlquist, founder of the Chesterton Schools Network, once said, “A school is not a Utopia; it is an arena for failure with recourse to Christ.
